sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities fell as a Magnificent Seven-led rout over ballooning AI capital spending, compounded by a spike in oil above **$100**, unwound the prior week's tech leadership. MSCI World eased roughly **-1%** **(approx., verify before merging)**, with MSCI Developed Markets similar and MSCI Emerging Markets around **-1.5%** **(approx., verify before merging)**. The S&P 500 slipped about **-0.6%** to around **7,412** **(approx., verify before merging)** and the Nasdaq lost roughly **-2%**, as the MAG7 shed nearly **$797bn** in a single session on Thursday. Europe's Euro Stoxx 50 finished broadly flat **(approx., verify before merging)** while the STOXX 600 held **+0.07%**. China's CSI 300 fell **-1.48%**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng tumbled **-5.24%** and Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped **-2.65%** to about **64,611**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities retreated, sharply reversing the previous week's mega-cap technology leadership. The S&P 500 eased to about **7,412**, the Nasdaq Composite slipped to roughly **24,976** for a weekly loss near **-2%**, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed around **51,947**, with information technology and communication services posting the steepest sector losses.

The MAG7 shed nearly **$797bn** in a single session on Thursday, the worst mega-cap day since the April 2025 tariff shock, as Alphabet lifted its 2026 capex guidance to as much as **$205bn** and fell **7.3%**, while a profit miss sent Tesla down **13%**. Microsoft, Amazon and Meta also declined as scrutiny of AI infrastructure spending intensified and the debate shifted from outlays to monetisation.

June CPI posted its largest monthly decline in more than six years, reinforcing a disinflation narrative, but a surge in oil above **$100** revived inflation concerns. The Fed is still expected to hold in July, though September has become a live meeting should energy-driven price pressures persist.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities ended a volatile week broadly unchanged as Friday's technology weakness in the US and Asia spread across the region. The pan-European STOXX Europe 600 rose just **0.07%** in local-currency terms, masking notable dispersion, while the Euro Stoxx 50 finished broadly flat **(approx., verify before merging)** as chip and AI-linked names tracked global peers lower.

Lower-tech, value-oriented indices held up better than growth-heavy bourses, with energy and defensive sectors cushioning the AI-led drawdown. The euro came under pressure after June inflation printed below expectations, and higher oil prices worsened the euro area's terms of trade, keeping the rates outlook firmly in focus.

With Brent briefly topping **$100**, rekindled inflation concerns reinforced a defensive tone across the region, leaving cyclical, technology-exposed markets lagging their more resilient, value-tilted peers.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets fell as a global semiconductor and AI selloff late in the week erased earlier gains. Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped **-2.65%** to roughly **64,611** and the broader TOPIX lost **-2.02%**; AI-related shares initially rallied on upbeat US chipmaker forecasts before a global technology rout prompted profit-taking.

Chinese equities also declined, with the mainland CSI 300 down **-1.48%** and the Shanghai Composite off **-1.55%** in local-currency terms, as an early rally in AI and semiconductor shares gave way to the broader regional pullback. Hong Kong underperformed sharply, with the Hang Seng tumbling **-5.24%** as weakness in large internet names deepened the technology-led decline.

The drawdown underscored how tightly regional sentiment remains tethered to the AI and chip cycle, leaving policy signals a secondary consideration as valuations and mega-cap capex plans dominated attention.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar stayed broadly firm, supported by higher-for-longer Fed expectations, resilient growth and a widening yield advantage across the G10, with oil above **$100** and renewed tariff risks adding to demand, even as positioning looked increasingly crowded.

Sterling consolidated after a strong summer rally, with softer risk sentiment, higher energy prices and lingering fiscal concerns overshadowing supportive domestic data, though GBP held near one-year highs against the euro. The euro itself came under pressure after June inflation printed below expectations and higher oil eroded the region's terms of trade.

The yen remained the standout underperformer, with USD/JPY climbing to its highest level since December 1986 near four-decade lows, weighed by higher oil and speculation that PM Takaichi would push back on further BoJ rate hikes, keeping intervention risk elevated.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy reasserted itself as the dominant cross-asset driver. Brent crude topped **$100** for the first time since May as a widening US-Iran conflict disrupted tanker traffic through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, with WTI trading in the high **$90s** before prices eased back below **$100** into Friday.

Gold retreated about **2%** to around **$4,030**, giving back an earlier advance towards **$4,130**, as higher real yields and revived rate-hike bets dulled the appeal of the non-yielding metal. Funds continued to trim exposure across both crude oil and precious metals despite the sharp price swings.

The higher-oil, sticky-inflation mix lifted sovereign yields and tightened financial conditions, sharpening the divergence between a resilient energy complex and a pressured metals sector and feeding back into equity and rates volatility.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign yields ground higher as rising oil and Middle East tensions revived inflation concerns. The 10-year UST broke above **4.70%** for the first time since January 2025 before finishing near **4.69%**, the 2-year ended around **4.33%**, and the 30-year revisited its May highs, the loftiest levels since 2007.

At roughly **4.33%**, the 2-year now exceeds the Fed policy rate by the widest margin since 2022, signalling that the market is beginning to price the possibility of hikes. Edward Jones expects the Fed to hold in July while flagging September as a live meeting, and sees the 10-year trading in a **4.5%**–**5.0%** range.

Credit was resilient but uneven, with HY pressured by geopolitics and higher oil before rising on soft CPI data and strong bank earnings, while IG held broadly steady, leaving quality and selectivity the prevailing themes amid elevated valuations.
